query: For HfNbTaTiZr refractory high-entropy alloy, earlier studies separately examined tensile creep at 1250 °C, microhardness changes during cold rolling, elastic moduli from 293 to 1100 K, and hardening after aging at 600–800 °C. However, these findings do not provide a unified explanation of the alloy’s stress–strain and thermoelastic behavior. Thermal expansion is also relevant because mismatch can produce thermal stresses during composite solidification and potentially affect strength. What single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain the unresolved behavior? Specify a controlled comparison that would isolate the governing cause, observations predicted relative to a baseline, the relevant temperature and response boundaries, how the earlier findings support the hypothesis, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The alloy’s unusual stress–strain and thermoelastic responses are governed by local lattice distortions that induce thermal expansion mismatches and, consequently, internal stresses. These stresses simultaneously influence high-temperature creep, elastic modulus variations, microhardness after deformation, and age hardening.
generation.material_initial_state: As-cast HfNbTaTiZr refractory high-entropy alloy with inherent atomic size differences that create local lattice distortions.
generation.intervention: Produce a modified version of the alloy by partially substituting one or more elements to reduce the atomic size mismatch (and hence the extent of lattice distortions), while keeping overall phase structure similar.
generation.conditions: Tests conducted from room temperature up to 1250 °C, including aging treatments at 600–800 °C. Comparisons are made between the standard alloy and the modified alloy under identical thermal and mechanical processing conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: Local lattice distortions that cause heterogeneous, thermally responsive expansion mismatches at microstructural interfaces.
generation.mechanism: Atomic size disparities in HfNbTaTiZr create inherent lattice distortions, which result in internal elastic heterogeneity. Upon heating, these distortions give rise to local thermal expansion mismatches that generate internal stresses. These stresses impede dislocation motion, modify the apparent elastic moduli, and influence creep behavior at high temperatures as well as post-aging hardening.
generation.predicted_outcome: Reducing the atomic size mismatch should decrease the internal mismatch stresses. Compared to the standard alloy, the modified alloy is predicted to show lower high-temperature creep rates, reduced age-induced hardening, and elastic moduli that more closely follow homogeneous theoretical predictions.
generation.baseline: Behavior of the standard HfNbTaTiZr alloy as observed in earlier separate studies (creep at 1250 °C, microhardness changes, elastic moduli variations, and hardening after aging).
generation.boundary: The hypothesis is expected to hold over the temperature range from 293 K to 1250 °C, with a pronounced influence in the aging regime from 600 °C to 800 °C. Outside these temperature regimes, other mechanisms may predominate.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative influence of reduced lattice distortions on mechanical parameters is uncertain because other operative mechanisms (such as secondary phase formation or additional microstructural heterogeneities) may also contribute to the observed behavior.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: the standard HfNbTaTiZr alloy and a compositionally modified version with reduced atomic size mismatch. Subject both sets to (a) tensile creep testing at 1250 °C, (b) elastic modulus measurements from 293 to 1100 K, and (c) aging at 600–800 °C followed by microhardness and hardening assessments. Ensure all other processing parameters are identical between the two groups.
measurements: Elastic moduli as a function of temperature
Microhardness before and after cold rolling
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the modified alloy does not show a statistically significant reduction in high-temperature creep rates, less pronounced age hardening, and elastic moduli that more closely align with homogeneous predictions compared to the standard alloy, then the dominance of local lattice distortions and thermal expansion mismatch as the governing mechanism is falsified.

cited_evidence.text:
Dual heterogeneous structures lead to ultrahigh strength and uniform ductility in a Co-Cr-Ni medium-entropy alloy

Abstract: Alloys with ultra-high strength and sufficient ductility are highly desired for modern engineering applications but difficult to develop. Here we report that, by a careful controlling alloy composition, thermomechanical process, and microstructural feature, a Co-Cr-Ni-based medium-entropy alloy (MEA) with a dual heterogeneous structure of both matrix and precipitates can be designed to provide an ultra-high tensile strength of 2.2 GPa and uniform elongation of 13% at ambient temperature, properties that are much improved over their counterparts without the heterogeneous structure. Electron microscopy characterizations reveal that the dual heterogeneous structures are composed of a heterogeneous matrix with both coarse grains (10∼30 μm) and ultra-fine grains (0.5∼2 μm), together with heterogeneous L12-structured nanoprecipitates ranging from several to hundreds of nanometers.
